papers.title: Physical Quantities and Units: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on physical quantities and units, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fundamental quantity?
questions.explanation:
The seven SI base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Electric current (the ampere) is one of them.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Force: Force is derived: $F = ma$ combines mass, length and time.
- Weight: Weight is a force ($W = mg$), so it is a derived quantity.
- Pressure: Pressure is force per unit area: a derived quantity.

questions.stem: The SI unit of power expressed in base units is
questions.explanation:
Power = work ÷ time. J = kg m² s⁻², so W = J s⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻³.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- kg m² s⁻²: That is the joule, the unit of energy. Power is energy per second, so divide by one more second.
- kg m s⁻²: That is the newton, the unit of force.
- kg m⁻¹ s⁻²: That is the pascal, the unit of pressure.

questions.stem: Which pair consists of a fundamental quantity and its correct SI unit?
questions.explanation:
Thermodynamic temperature is a base quantity and its SI unit is the kelvin (K).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- temperature, degree Celsius: The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin, not the degree Celsius.
- mass, gram: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram.
- length, centimetre: The SI unit of length is the metre.

questions.stem: Express a speed of 90 km h⁻¹ in m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation:
$90\ \text{km h}^{-1} = \dfrac{90 \times 1000\ \text{m}}{3600\ \text{s}} = 25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (divide by 3.6).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2.5 m s⁻¹: You divided by 36 instead of 3.6.
- 324 m s⁻¹: You multiplied by 3.6 instead of dividing.
- 90000 m s⁻¹: You converted kilometres to metres but forgot to change hours to seconds.

questions.stem: A cube of side 2 cm has a mass of 64 g. What is its density in kg m⁻³?
questions.explanation:
Volume $= 2^3 = 8\ \text{cm}^3$, so density $= \dfrac{64}{8} = 8\ \text{g cm}^{-3} = 8000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8 kg m⁻³: That is the density in g cm⁻³. Multiply by 1000 to get kg m⁻³.
- 800 kg m⁻³: Check the conversion: 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, not 100.
- 16000 kg m⁻³: You took the volume as 2 × 2 = 4 cm³. The volume of a cube is side³ = 8 cm³.

questions.stem: The dimensions of pressure are
questions.explanation:
$[p] = \dfrac{[F]}{[A]} = \dfrac{\text{M L T}^{-2}}{\text{L}^2} = \text{M L}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- M L T⁻²: Those are the dimensions of force. Pressure is force divided by area (L²).
- M L² T⁻²: Those are the dimensions of energy.
- M L⁻³: Those are the dimensions of density.

questions.stem: Which quantity has the dimensions M L T⁻¹?
questions.explanation:
Momentum $= mv$, so $[p] = \text{M} \times \text{L T}^{-1} = \text{M L T}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- force: Force has dimensions M L T⁻² (mass × acceleration).
- power: Power has dimensions M L² T⁻³.
- acceleration: Acceleration has dimensions L T⁻²; it has no mass dimension.

questions.stem: 1 microfarad is equal to
questions.explanation:
The prefix micro (μ) means 10⁻⁶, so 1 μF = 10⁻⁶ F.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10⁻³ F: That is a millifarad. Micro means 10⁻⁶.
- 10⁻⁹ F: That is a nanofarad.
- 10⁻¹² F: That is a picofarad.

papers.title: Scalars and Vectors: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on scalars and vectors, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation:
Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- speed: Speed has magnitude only. Velocity is its vector partner.
- energy: Energy has no direction: it is a scalar.
- density: Density is mass per unit volume, a scalar.

questions.stem: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act on a body at right angles to each other. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.explanation:
For perpendicular forces, $R = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 14 N: You added the forces as if they acted in the same direction.
- 2 N: You subtracted them as if they acted in opposite directions.
- 48 N: You multiplied the forces.

questions.stem: A force of 40 N acts at 60° to the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
questions.explanation:
Horizontal component $= F\cos\theta = 40\cos 60° = 40 \times 0.5 = 20\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 34.6 N: You used sine. The horizontal component is next to the 60° angle, so use cosine.
- 40 N: The whole force is not horizontal; only its component $F\cos\theta$ is.
- 80 N: You divided by cos 60° instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A man walks 12 m due east and then 5 m due north. What is his displacement from the starting point?
questions.explanation:
Displacement $= \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13\ \text{m}$ (north of east).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 17 m: 17 m is the distance walked, not the displacement.
- 7 m: You subtracted the two walks.
- 10.9 m: Pythagoras adds the squares: $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2}$.

questions.stem: Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act at a point. Which of the following CANNOT be the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.explanation:
The resultant of 5 N and 3 N lies between $5 - 3 = 2$ N and $5 + 3 = 8$ N. 9 N is outside this range.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2 N: 2 N is possible: the forces act in opposite directions.
- 8 N: 8 N is possible: the forces act in the same direction.
- 5 N: 5 N is possible at a suitable angle between the forces.

questions.stem: The equilibrant of a set of forces is
questions.explanation:
The equilibrant is the single force that brings the system into equilibrium: equal and opposite to the resultant.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- equal in magnitude and direction to their resultant: That describes the resultant itself, not the force that balances it.
- the sum of the magnitudes of the forces: Vectors are not added by adding magnitudes.
- always perpendicular to their resultant: A perpendicular force cannot cancel the resultant.

options.label: A
options.content: equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to their resultant

options.label: B
options.content: equal in magnitude and direction to their resultant

options.label: C
options.content: the sum of the magnitudes of the forces

questions.stem: A canoe heads straight across a river at 4 m s⁻¹ while the current flows at 3 m s⁻¹. What is the canoe's resultant speed?
questions.explanation:
$v = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 7 m s⁻¹: The velocities are perpendicular, so they do not simply add.
- 1 m s⁻¹: You subtracted the speeds.
- 2.65 m s⁻¹: That is $\sqrt{4^2 - 3^2}$, the speed straight across when steering upstream to land opposite.

questions.stem: Two cars move towards each other along a straight road at 20 m s⁻¹ and 15 m s⁻¹. What is the velocity of one relative to the other?
questions.explanation:
Moving in opposite directions, each sees the other approach at $20 + 15 = 35$ m s⁻¹.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 m s⁻¹: That would be their relative speed if they moved in the same direction.
- 25 m s⁻¹: That is $\sqrt{20^2 + 15^2}$; the velocities are along the same line, not perpendicular.
- 17.5 m s⁻¹: You averaged the speeds.

papers.title: Measurement and Errors: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on measurement and errors, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a thin wire?
questions.explanation:
A micrometer screw gauge reads to 0.01 mm, suitable for a wire's diameter.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- metre rule: A metre rule reads only to about 1 mm, far too coarse for a wire.
- vernier calipers: Vernier calipers read to 0.01 cm (0.1 mm); a wire needs the finer 0.01 mm of a micrometer.
- measuring tape: A tape is for long lengths.

questions.stem: On a vernier caliper the main scale reading is 2.3 cm and the 7th vernier division coincides with a main scale division. If the vernier constant is 0.01 cm, what is the reading?
questions.explanation:
Reading $= 2.3 + 7 \times 0.01 = 2.37\ \text{cm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2.307 cm: Each vernier division is worth 0.01 cm, so 7 divisions add 0.07 cm, not 0.007 cm.
- 3.0 cm: You added 0.7 cm. Seven vernier divisions add 7 × 0.01 = 0.07 cm.
- 2.23 cm: The vernier reading is added to, not subtracted from, the main scale reading.

questions.stem: A micrometer has a sleeve reading of 5.5 mm and the 28th thimble division is on the datum line. Each thimble division is 0.01 mm. What is the reading?
questions.explanation:
Reading $= 5.5 + 28 \times 0.01 = 5.78\ \text{mm}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5.528 mm: Each thimble division is 0.01 mm, so 28 divisions are 0.28 mm, not 0.028 mm.
- 8.3 mm: 28 thimble divisions are 0.28 mm, not 2.8 mm.
- 5.22 mm: The thimble reading is added to the sleeve reading.

questions.stem: Parallax error in reading a scale is avoided by
questions.explanation:
Parallax arises when the eye views the scale at an angle; looking perpendicularly at the mark removes it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- taking readings very quickly: Speed does not change the angle of viewing.
- using a longer scale: A longer scale does not remove the effect of viewing at an angle.
- repeating the reading many times from the same position: Repeating from the same wrong angle repeats the same systematic error.

options.label: A
options.content: placing the eye directly in line with the mark being read

options.label: D
options.content: repeating the reading many times from the same position

questions.stem: A zero error on a measuring instrument produces
questions.explanation:
A zero error affects every reading in the same way, so it is systematic. Correct it by subtracting (or adding) the zero reading.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a random error: Random errors vary unpredictably; a zero error shifts every reading by the same amount.
- a parallax error: Parallax comes from the angle of viewing, not from the instrument's zero.
- no error if readings are repeated: Repeating readings cannot remove an error that is the same each time.

options.label: C
options.content: no error if readings are repeated

questions.stem: The length of a rod is recorded as (50.0 ± 0.5) cm. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation:
Percentage error $= \dfrac{0.5}{50.0} \times 100\% = 1\%$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.5 %: 0.5 is the absolute error in cm, not the percentage.
- 10 %: Percentage error is 0.5 ÷ 50 × 100, not 0.5 ÷ 5 × 100.
- 0.01 %: You found the fractional error but did not multiply by 100.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are there in 0.004050?
questions.explanation:
Ignore the leading zeros. The significant figures are 4, 0, 5, 0: four in all.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 7: Leading zeros before the first non-zero digit are not significant.
- 3: The final zero after the 5 is significant, because it comes after the decimal point.
- 6: Only the zeros after the first non-zero digit count: 4, 0, 5, 0.

questions.stem: Repeating a measurement several times and taking the mean reduces
questions.explanation:
Random errors scatter readings both ways, so they partly cancel when the mean is taken.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- systematic errors: A systematic error shifts every reading the same way; averaging keeps it.
- zero errors: A zero error is systematic; it must be corrected, not averaged away.
- the resolution of the instrument: Averaging does not change the instrument's smallest division.

papers.title: Motion in a Straight Line: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on motion in a straight line, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The gradient of a displacement–time graph gives
questions.explanation:
Gradient = change in displacement ÷ time = velocity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- acceleration: Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
- distance travelled: Displacement is read from the graph's height, not from its gradient.
- force: A motion graph alone does not give force.

questions.stem: The area under a velocity–time graph represents
questions.explanation:
Area = velocity × time = displacement (distance for one-way motion).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- acceleration: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph, not the area.
- speed: Speed is read directly off the velocity axis.
- time: Time is on the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: A runner covers 400 m in 50 s and then 200 m in 30 s. What is her average speed for the whole run?
questions.explanation:
Average speed $= \dfrac{400 + 200}{50 + 30} = \dfrac{600}{80} = 7.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 7.33 m s⁻¹: You averaged the two speeds. Average speed is total distance ÷ total time.
- 8 m s⁻¹: That is the speed for the first part only.
- 12 m s⁻¹: You divided total distance by the first time only.

questions.stem: A car's velocity changes from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation:
$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{30 - 10}{4} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10 m s⁻²: You divided the change in velocity by 2 instead of by the time, 4 s.
- 7.5 m s⁻²: You divided the final velocity by the time; subtract the initial velocity first.
- 80 m s⁻²: You multiplied the change in velocity by the time.

questions.stem: A horizontal straight line on a velocity–time graph shows that the body is
questions.explanation:
Constant velocity means zero gradient: a horizontal line above the time axis.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- at rest: At rest, the line would lie along the time axis (velocity zero).
- accelerating uniformly: Uniform acceleration gives a sloping straight line.
- decelerating: Deceleration gives a line sloping downwards.

questions.stem: A keke goes once round a circular track at constant speed and returns to its starting point. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
Ending at the start point gives zero displacement, while the distance is the circumference of the track.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Its displacement equals the distance travelled.  
  Displacement is measured in a straight line from start to finish; the keke ended where it began.
- Its velocity was constant throughout.  
  Its direction kept changing, so its velocity changed.
- Its average speed is zero.  
  Average speed is distance ÷ time, which is not zero.

options.label: A
options.content: Its displacement is zero but the distance travelled is not.

options.label: B
options.content: Its displacement equals the distance travelled.

questions.stem: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. Using a velocity–time graph, find the distance covered.
questions.explanation:
Distance = area of triangle $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 12 = 36\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 72 m: You took the area as a rectangle (12 × 6). The graph is a triangle: use ½ × base × height.
- 2 m: That is the acceleration (12 ÷ 6), not the distance.
- 18 m: You halved twice.

questions.stem: A train moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest uniformly in 25 s. What is its deceleration?
questions.explanation:
$a = \dfrac{0 - 20}{25} = -0.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, a deceleration of 0.8 m s⁻².

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.25 m s⁻²: You divided the time by the velocity.
- 500 m s⁻²: You multiplied the velocity by the time.
- 1.6 m s⁻²: You doubled the result; deceleration is simply (20 − 0) ÷ 25.

papers.title: Equations of Motion: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on equations of motion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² for 10 s. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation:
$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(3)(10)^2 = 150\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 300 m: You forgot the ½ in $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.
- 30 m: That is the final velocity, $v = at$, not the distance.
- 15 m: You used $t$ instead of $t^2$.

questions.stem: A car travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly and stops in 90 m. What is its deceleration?
questions.explanation:
$0 = 30^2 + 2a(90) \Rightarrow a = -\dfrac{900}{180} = -5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$: a deceleration of 5 m s⁻².

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10 m s⁻²: You forgot the 2 in $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
- 0.33 m s⁻²: You divided the speed by the distance.
- 2.5 m s⁻²: You used 4 instead of 2 in the denominator.

questions.stem: A motorcycle moving at 10 m s⁻¹ accelerates at 2 m s⁻² over 75 m. What is its final velocity?
questions.explanation:
$v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 100 + 2(2)(75) = 400 \Rightarrow v = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 15.8 m s⁻¹: You left out the acceleration: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ needs $2 \times 2 \times 75$.
- 400 m s⁻¹: That is $v^2$. Take the square root.
- 17.3 m s⁻¹: You left out the initial velocity $u^2$.

questions.stem: Which equation would you use to find the final velocity of a uniformly accelerating body when the time is not known?
questions.explanation:
$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ is the only equation of motion without $t$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $v = u + at$: This needs the time $t$.
- $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: This contains $t$ and does not contain $v$.
- $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$: This needs the time $t$.

questions.stem: A taxi at 15 m s⁻¹ has a driver with a reaction time of 0.6 s. After reacting, the brakes give a deceleration of 5 m s⁻². What is the total stopping distance?
questions.explanation:
Thinking: $15 \times 0.6 = 9$ m. Braking: $\dfrac{15^2}{2 \times 5} = 22.5$ m. Total $= 31.5$ m.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 22.5 m: That is the braking distance only. Add the thinking distance, 15 × 0.6 = 9 m.
- 9 m: That is the thinking distance only.
- 54 m: You forgot the 2 in the braking distance $u^2/2a$.

questions.stem: A body moving with uniform acceleration has velocity 4 m s⁻¹ at one instant and 16 m s⁻¹ six seconds later. How far does it travel in those 6 s?
questions.explanation:
$s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t = \tfrac{1}{2}(4 + 16)(6) = 60\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 96 m: You used the final velocity × time. Use the average velocity, (4 + 16) ÷ 2.
- 24 m: You used the initial velocity × time.
- 36 m: You used the change in velocity, (16 − 4), × ½ × 6.

questions.stem: A police motorcycle starts from rest with acceleration 4 m s⁻² at the moment a car passes it at a steady 20 m s⁻¹. After what time does the motorcycle catch the car?
questions.explanation:
Car: $s = 20t$. Motorcycle: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(4)t^2 = 2t^2$. $2t^2 = 20t \Rightarrow t = 10\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 s: That is when the motorcycle's speed equals the car's (4t = 20), not when it catches up.
- 20 s: You forgot the ½ in $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: solve $2t^2 = 20t$.
- 3.16 s: Set the displacements equal: $2t^2 = 20t$, which gives $t = 10$ s.

questions.stem: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration 2 m s⁻². How far does it travel during the 5th second?
questions.explanation:
$s_5 - s_4 = \tfrac{1}{2}(2)(25) - \tfrac{1}{2}(2)(16) = 25 - 16 = 9\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 25 m: That is the distance in the first 5 seconds, not in the 5th second alone.
- 16 m: That is the distance in the first 4 seconds.
- 10 m: That is the velocity at the end of the 5th second.

papers.title: Motion under Gravity: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on motion under gravity, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A stone is dropped from rest from a height of 45 m. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow 45 = 5t^2 \Rightarrow t = 3\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.5 s: You used $h = gt$; the correct equation is $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$.
- 9 s: That is $t^2$. Take the square root.
- 2.12 s: You forgot the ½: $45 = 5t^2$, not $10t^2$.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a speed of 25 m s⁻¹. What is the maximum height reached? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g} = \dfrac{625}{20} = 31.25\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 62.5 m: You forgot the 2 in $H = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$.
- 2.5 m: That is the time to the top, $u/g$, not the height.
- 125 m: You divided by 5 instead of by 2g = 20.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m s⁻¹ and caught at the same height. What is its total time in the air? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Time of flight $= \dfrac{2u}{g} = \dfrac{40}{10} = 4\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2 s: That is the time to reach the top. The ball takes the same time to come down.
- 20 s: That is the maximum height, $u^2/2g$, in metres.
- 8 s: You doubled twice.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. At its highest point, its
questions.explanation:
At the top the ball stops momentarily (v = 0), but its weight still gives it an acceleration $g$ downwards.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- velocity and acceleration are both zero: If the acceleration were zero, the ball would stay at the top. Gravity still acts.
- velocity is maximum and its acceleration is zero: The velocity is zero at the top, and gravity still accelerates it.
- acceleration is zero and its velocity is g: Velocity and acceleration are mixed up here; $g$ is the acceleration.

options.label: A
options.content: velocity is zero and its acceleration is g downwards

options.label: B
options.content: velocity and acceleration are both zero

options.label: C
options.content: velocity is maximum and its acceleration is zero

options.label: D
options.content: acceleration is zero and its velocity is g

questions.stem: In a vacuum, a feather and a stone are released together from the same height. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
In a vacuum only gravity acts, and every body falls with acceleration $g$, whatever its mass.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- The stone lands first because it is heavier.  
  Without air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration $g$.
- The feather lands first because it is lighter.  
  Lighter bodies do not fall faster.
- The feather floats and does not fall.  
  With no air, nothing supports the feather; it falls freely.

options.label: A
options.content: The stone lands first because it is heavier.

options.label: B
options.content: The feather lands first because it is lighter.

options.label: C
options.content: The feather floats and does not fall.

options.label: D
options.content: They reach the ground at the same time.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 30 m s⁻¹. What is its velocity after 4 s? (Take upwards as positive; g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$v = u - gt = 30 - 10(4) = -10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: 10 m s⁻¹ downwards.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10 m s⁻¹: The magnitude is right, but after 3 s the stone is falling, so its velocity is negative (downwards).
- 70 m s⁻¹: You added gravity's effect instead of subtracting it: $v = u - gt$.
- -40 m s⁻¹: You used $v = -gt$ and ignored the initial velocity.

questions.stem: A body falls freely from rest. What is its speed after falling 20 m? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$v^2 = 2gh = 2(10)(20) = 400 \Rightarrow v = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 400 m s⁻¹: That is $v^2$. Take the square root.
- 14.1 m s⁻¹: You forgot the 2 in $v^2 = 2gh$.
- 200 m s⁻¹: You multiplied g by h without the 2 or the square root.

questions.stem: A skydiver falling through air reaches terminal velocity when
questions.explanation:
When air resistance balances the weight, the resultant force is zero, so she falls at a constant (terminal) velocity.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- her weight becomes zero: Her weight ($mg$) does not change as she falls.
- air resistance becomes zero: Air resistance grows with speed; it is at its largest at terminal velocity.
- her acceleration equals g: At terminal velocity her acceleration is zero.

papers.title: Projectile Motion: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on projectile motion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: For a projectile (air resistance neglected), which quantity remains constant throughout the flight?
questions.explanation:
No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity $u\cos\theta$ never changes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the vertical component of velocity: Gravity changes the vertical velocity by $g$ every second.
- the speed: The speed is least at the top and greater elsewhere.
- the kinetic energy: Kinetic energy changes as the speed changes.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ off a cliff 80 m high. How far from the foot of the cliff does it land? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Fall time: $80 = 5t^2 \Rightarrow t = 4\ \text{s}$. Distance $= 12 \times 4 = 48\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 96 m: You took the fall time as 8 s; $80 = 5t^2$ gives $t = 4$ s.
- 4 m: That is the time of fall, not the distance.
- 33.9 m: You forgot the ½: $80 = 5t^2$, not $10t^2$.

questions.stem: A stone is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. What is its time of flight? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2(20)(0.5)}{10} = 2\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1 s: That is the time to the highest point; the flight lasts twice as long.
- 3.46 s: You used cos 30°. The vertical component is $u\sin\theta$.
- 4 s: You used the full speed 20 m s⁻¹ as the vertical velocity.

questions.stem: For a given speed of projection, the horizontal range on level ground is greatest when the angle of projection is
questions.explanation:
$R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ is greatest when $\sin 2\theta = 1$, so $\theta = 45°$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 90°: At 90° the body goes straight up and comes straight down: zero range.
- 30°: 30° gives less range than 45°, because $\sin 60° < \sin 90°$.
- 60°: 60° gives the same range as 30°, less than at 45°.

questions.stem: A ball is projected at 30 m s⁻¹ at 60° to the horizontal. What is its speed at the highest point of its path?
questions.explanation:
At the top, speed $= u\cos\theta = 30\cos 60° = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0 m s⁻¹: Only the vertical velocity is zero at the top; the horizontal velocity remains.
- 26.0 m s⁻¹: That is the initial vertical component, which is zero at the top.
- 30 m s⁻¹: The speed at the top equals only the horizontal component, $u\cos\theta$.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 40 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the horizontal. What is its maximum height? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$H = \dfrac{(u\sin\theta)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{(40 \times 0.5)^2}{20} = \dfrac{400}{20} = 20\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 80 m: You used the full speed instead of the vertical component $u\sin\theta$.
- 40 m: You forgot the 2 in $H = \dfrac{(u\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$.
- 60 m: You used cos 30° instead of sin 30°.

questions.stem: What is the maximum range of a projectile launched at 20 m s⁻¹ on level ground? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Maximum range (at 45°) $= \dfrac{u^2}{g} = \dfrac{400}{10} = 40\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20 m: You divided by 2g; maximum range is $u^2/g$.
- 80 m: You doubled the range; $R_{max} = u^2/g$.
- 2 m: That is $u/g$, a time-like quantity, not the range.

questions.stem: Which pair of angles of projection gives the same horizontal range for the same speed?
questions.explanation:
$\sin 2\theta$ is the same for complementary angles: $\sin 40° = \sin 140°$, so 20° and 70° give equal ranges.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20° and 40°: Equal ranges need angles that add up to 90°.
- 30° and 45°: These do not add up to 90°; 45° gives the larger range.
- 60° and 120°: 120° is not a launch angle above the horizontal in the same direction.

papers.title: Newton's Laws of Motion: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on newton's laws of motion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Passengers in a bus jerk forward when it stops suddenly. This is explained by
questions.explanation:
By Newton's first law, a moving body keeps moving unless a force acts. The bus stops, but the passengers' bodies tend to continue: inertia.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- friction: Friction acts between surfaces; it does not explain why the body keeps moving.
- Newton's third law: The third law is about action–reaction pairs, not about bodies continuing to move.
- gravity: Gravity acts downwards, not forwards.

questions.stem: A resultant force of 60 N acts on a mass of 12 kg. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation:
$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{60}{12} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 720 m s⁻²: You multiplied force by mass. $a = F/m$.
- 0.2 m s⁻²: You divided mass by force.
- 72 m s⁻²: You added force and mass.

questions.stem: A box of mass 20 kg is pushed with a horizontal force of 150 N against a friction force of 50 N. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Resultant force $= 150 - 50 = 100\ \text{N}$; $a = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 7.5 m s⁻²: You ignored friction. Use the resultant force, 150 − 50.
- 10 m s⁻²: You added the friction instead of subtracting it.
- 2.5 m s⁻²: You used friction as the resultant force.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is stopped by a goalkeeper in 0.1 s. What is the average force on his hands?
questions.explanation:
$F = \dfrac{mv - mu}{t} = \dfrac{0.5 \times 20}{0.1} = 100\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 10 N: That is the change in momentum (N s), not the force.
- 1 N: You multiplied the momentum by the time instead of dividing.
- 200 N: You divided by 0.05 instead of 0.1.

questions.stem: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley and they move off together. What is their common velocity?
questions.explanation:
$3(4) + 1(0) = (3 + 1)v \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4 m s⁻¹: Momentum is shared with the extra mass, so the velocity must fall.
- 12 m s⁻¹: That is the total momentum, not the velocity.
- 1.33 m s⁻¹: You divided the original velocity by 3. Divide the total momentum (12) by the combined mass, 4 kg.

questions.stem: A gun of mass 5 kg fires a bullet of mass 25 g at 400 m s⁻¹. What is the recoil speed of the gun?
questions.explanation:
Total momentum stays zero: $0.025 \times 400 = 5v \Rightarrow v = 2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2000 m s⁻¹: You used 25 kg for the bullet. 25 g = 0.025 kg.
- 80 m s⁻¹: You multiplied the bullet's speed by 1/5 without using the bullet's mass.
- 0.2 m s⁻¹: Recoil speed = bullet momentum ÷ gun mass = 10 ÷ 5.

questions.stem: A 50 kg girl stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating upwards at 2 m s⁻². What does the scale read? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$R - mg = ma \Rightarrow R = m(g + a) = 50(10 + 2) = 600\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 500 N: That is her weight at rest. Accelerating upwards, the scale reads more.
- 400 N: You subtracted; for upward acceleration $R = m(g + a)$.
- 100 N: That is only the extra force $ma$.

questions.stem: A book rests on a table. The reaction to the weight of the book is
questions.explanation:
The weight is the Earth pulling the book. Its third-law partner is the book pulling the Earth, equal and opposite.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the upward push of the table on the book: That force acts on the same body (the book); action and reaction act on different bodies.
- the downward push of the book on the table: That is the reaction to the table's push on the book.
- the friction between the book and the table: No friction acts on a book resting on a level table.

options.label: A
options.content: the upward pull of the book on the Earth

options.label: B
options.content: the upward push of the table on the book

options.label: C
options.content: the downward push of the book on the table

options.label: D
options.content: the friction between the book and the table

papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on equilibrium of forces, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A body acted on by several concurrent forces is in equilibrium when
questions.explanation:
Equilibrium requires zero resultant force, so that the body has no acceleration.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- all the forces are equal in magnitude: Unequal forces can balance, and equal ones need not.
- the forces all act in the same direction: Forces in one direction cannot balance.
- the body is moving with uniform acceleration: Equilibrium means zero acceleration.

options.label: A
options.content: all the forces are equal in magnitude

options.label: B
options.content: the forces all act in the same direction

options.label: C
options.content: the body is moving with uniform acceleration

options.label: D
options.content: the resultant of the forces is zero

questions.stem: A lamp of weight 30 N hangs from the midpoint of a wire. Each half of the wire makes 30° with the horizontal. What is the tension in the wire?
questions.explanation:
$2T\sin 30° = 30 \Rightarrow 2T(0.5) = 30 \Rightarrow T = 30\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 15 N: You forgot that the vertical component is $T\sin 30°$, which is half of $T$.
- 17.3 N: You used cos 30°; the vertical component is $T\sin 30°$.
- 60 N: There are two halves of wire sharing the load: $2T\sin 30° = 30$.

questions.stem: A 50 N block rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30°. What force parallel to the plane holds it at rest?
questions.explanation:
Force $= mg\sin\theta = 50\sin 30° = 25\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 43.3 N: That is $mg\cos\theta$, the component into the plane.
- 50 N: Only the component of weight along the plane needs balancing.
- 100 N: You divided by sin 30° instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Lami's theorem states that when three concurrent forces are in equilibrium, each force is proportional to
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \dfrac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \dfrac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$, where each angle lies between the other two forces.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the cosine of the angle between the other two forces: The theorem uses sines, as in the sine rule.
- the angle between the other two forces: It is the sine of the angle, not the angle itself.
- the sum of the other two forces: The forces are vectors; their magnitudes do not simply add.

options.label: A
options.content: the sine of the angle between the other two forces

options.label: B
options.content: the cosine of the angle between the other two forces

options.label: C
options.content: the angle between the other two forces

options.label: D
options.content: the sum of the other two forces

questions.stem: A 100 N weight hangs from two strings at right angles to each other. One string makes 30° with the vertical. What is the tension in that string?
questions.explanation:
By Lami's theorem: $\dfrac{T_1}{\sin 120°} = \dfrac{100}{\sin 90°} \Rightarrow T_1 = 100 \times 0.866 = 86.6\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 50 N: That is the tension in the other string, which makes 60° with the vertical.
- 100 N: The weight is shared between the two strings.
- 115.5 N: You divided by cos 30°. With the strings at 90°, $T_1 = 100\cos 30°$.

questions.stem: Three forces acting at a point are in equilibrium. If they are drawn to scale nose to tail, they form
questions.explanation:
Triangle of forces: three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn in order.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a straight line: A straight line arises only if all three forces are parallel.
- an open triangle with a gap equal to the resultant: In equilibrium there is no resultant, so no gap.
- a right-angled triangle in every case: The triangle can have any shape.

options.label: B
options.content: an open triangle with a gap equal to the resultant

options.label: C
options.content: a right-angled triangle in every case

questions.stem: Forces of 9 N east and 12 N north act on a particle. What is the magnitude of the equilibrant?
questions.explanation:
Resultant $= \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = 15$ N; the equilibrant has the same size, opposite direction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 21 N: You added the magnitudes directly; the forces are perpendicular.
- 3 N: You subtracted the magnitudes.
- 7.94 N: Pythagoras adds the squares: $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2}$.

questions.stem: A 20 N box hangs on a rope. A horizontal force pulls it aside until the rope makes 45° with the vertical. What is the horizontal force?
questions.explanation:
Vertically $T\cos 45° = 20$; horizontally $P = T\sin 45°$. So $P = 20\tan 45° = 20\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 28.3 N: That is the tension in the rope, $20/\cos 45°$.
- 10 N: Horizontal force $= W\tan 45° = 20 \times 1$.
- 14.1 N: You multiplied by sin 45°; use $\tan 45°$.

papers.title: Moments and Turning Effects: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on moments and turning effects, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A force of 25 N is applied at right angles to a spanner, 0.4 m from the nut. What is the moment about the nut?
questions.explanation:
Moment $= F \times d = 25 \times 0.4 = 10\ \text{N m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 62.5 N m: You divided force by distance; moment = force × distance.
- 25.4 N m: You added force and distance.
- 100 N m: You used 4 m instead of 0.4 m.

questions.stem: A see-saw is balanced at its centre. A 400 N boy sits 1.5 m from the pivot. How far from the pivot must a 300 N girl sit on the other side to balance him?
questions.explanation:
$400 \times 1.5 = 300 \times d \Rightarrow d = 2\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.125 m: You inverted the ratio. The lighter girl must sit further away.
- 1.5 m: Equal distances balance only equal weights.
- 1.33 m: You found only the ratio of the weights. Multiply by the boy's distance: 400 × 1.5 = 300 × d.

questions.stem: The principle of moments states that for a body in equilibrium
questions.explanation:
Equilibrium means no turning: clockwise moments balance anticlockwise moments about any point.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the clockwise forces equal the anticlockwise forces: The principle is about moments (force × distance), not forces.
- all the forces act through the pivot: Forces need not act through the pivot.
- the moments about the pivot are all zero: Individual moments need not be zero; only their total.

options.label: A
options.content: the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point

options.label: B
options.content: the clockwise forces equal the anticlockwise forces

options.label: C
options.content: all the forces act through the pivot

options.label: D
options.content: the moments about the pivot are all zero

questions.stem: A uniform metre rule of weight 1.2 N is pivoted at the 30 cm mark. What weight must hang at the 10 cm mark to keep it horizontal?
questions.explanation:
The rule's weight acts at 50 cm, 20 cm from the pivot. $W \times 20 = 1.2 \times 20 \Rightarrow W = 1.2\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2.4 N: The rule's weight acts at the 50 cm mark, 20 cm from the pivot, not 10 cm.
- 0.6 N: Both distances are 20 cm, so the weights are equal.
- 3.0 N: Measure distances from the pivot (30 cm mark), not from the end.

questions.stem: A uniform plank 4 m long weighing 200 N rests on supports at its two ends. A 600 N man stands 1 m from the left end. What is the reaction at the right support?
questions.explanation:
Moments about the left end: $R \times 4 = 600 \times 1 + 200 \times 2 = 1000 \Rightarrow R = 250\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 550 N: That is the reaction at the left support.
- 400 N: The two supports do not share the load equally; the man is nearer the left.
- 150 N: You left out the plank's own weight.

questions.stem: A body is in stable equilibrium if, when slightly displaced,
questions.explanation:
In stable equilibrium, displacement raises the centre of gravity, and the weight's moment returns the body.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its centre of gravity is lowered and it falls over: That describes unstable equilibrium.
- its centre of gravity stays at the same height: That describes neutral equilibrium.
- its weight becomes zero: Displacing a body does not change its weight.

options.label: A
options.content: its centre of gravity is lowered and it falls over

options.label: B
options.content: its centre of gravity stays at the same height

options.label: D
options.content: its centre of gravity is raised and it returns to its original position

questions.stem: Which of these increases the stability of a vehicle?
questions.explanation:
A low centre of gravity and a wide base keep the line of action of the weight inside the base even when tilted.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a high centre of gravity and a narrow base: Both make overturning easier.
- loading heavy goods on the roof rack: That raises the centre of gravity.
- a high centre of gravity and a wide base: A high centre of gravity reduces stability.

options.label: A
options.content: a low centre of gravity and a wide wheel base

options.label: B
options.content: a high centre of gravity and a narrow base

options.label: C
options.content: loading heavy goods on the roof rack

options.label: D
options.content: a high centre of gravity and a wide base

questions.stem: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 15 N act on the rim of a steering wheel of diameter 0.4 m. What is the moment of the couple?
questions.explanation:
Moment of couple $= F \times d = 15 \times 0.4 = 6\ \text{N m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3 N m: You used the radius. The moment of a couple uses the distance between the forces (the diameter).
- 12 N m: You doubled the force; use one force × the distance between them.
- 37.5 N m: You divided by the diameter.

papers.title: Friction: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on friction, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A 40 kg crate rests on a floor. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. What horizontal force just starts it moving? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$F = \mu R = \mu mg = 0.5 \times 40 \times 10 = 200\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20 N: You used the mass instead of the weight: $R = mg = 400$ N.
- 400 N: That is the normal reaction; friction is $\mu R$.
- 800 N: You divided by μ instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A force of 30 N just makes a 60 N block start sliding on a horizontal bench. What is the coefficient of static friction?
questions.explanation:
$\mu = \dfrac{F}{R} = \dfrac{30}{60} = 0.5$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 2: You divided the weight by the force.
- 30: That is the friction force, not the coefficient.
- 90: You added the forces.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a law of solid friction?
questions.explanation:
Friction is independent of the area of contact (for the same normal reaction).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Friction opposes relative motion between the surfaces.  
  This is a law of friction.
- Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction.  
  This is a law of friction.
- Friction depends on the nature of the surfaces.  
  This is a law of friction.

options.label: A
options.content: Friction opposes relative motion between the surfaces.

options.label: B
options.content: Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction.

options.label: C
options.content: Friction depends on the nature of the surfaces.

options.label: D
options.content: Friction is directly proportional to the area of contact.

questions.stem: A block on a plank just begins to slide when the plank is tilted to 30°. What is the coefficient of static friction?
questions.explanation:
At the angle of friction, $\mu = \tan\theta = \tan 30° = 0.58$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.5: That is $\sin 30°$; the coefficient is $\tan\theta$.
- 0.87: That is $\cos 30°$; the coefficient is $\tan\theta$.
- 1.73: That is $\tan 60°$; use the angle of the plank, 30°.

questions.stem: Ball bearings are used in machines mainly to
questions.explanation:
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, so ball bearings reduce wear and wasted energy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase friction so parts grip: Bearings are fitted to reduce friction.
- increase the weight of the machine: Their purpose has nothing to do with weight.
- conduct heat away from the machine: That is not their main purpose.

options.label: A
options.content: reduce friction by replacing sliding with rolling

options.label: C
options.content: increase the weight of the machine

options.label: D
options.content: conduct heat away from the machine

questions.stem: A 10 kg box is pulled along a floor by a horizontal force of 80 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. What is its acceleration? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Friction $= 0.3 \times 100 = 30$ N. Resultant $= 80 - 30 = 50$ N. $a = \dfrac{50}{10} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8 m s⁻²: You ignored friction.
- 11 m s⁻²: You added friction to the pull.
- 3 m s⁻²: You used friction as the resultant force.

questions.stem: Compared with limiting (static) friction between the same surfaces, kinetic friction is
questions.explanation:
It takes more force to start a body sliding than to keep it sliding: kinetic friction is slightly less than limiting friction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- slightly greater: Once sliding starts, friction drops a little; that is why starting a heavy box is harder.
- exactly equal: Kinetic friction is usually a little smaller.
- zero: Sliding surfaces still experience friction.

questions.stem: A car of mass 800 kg skids to a stop from 20 m s⁻¹ on a road where the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.5. What is the stopping distance? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Deceleration $= \mu g = 0.5 \times 10 = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. $s = \dfrac{u^2}{2a} = \dfrac{400}{10} = 40\ \text{m}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 20 m: You forgot the 2 in $s = \dfrac{u^2}{2a}$.
- 80 m: You used μ = 0.25 by mistake; deceleration = μg = 5 m s⁻².
- 4 m: That is the stopping time, 20 ÷ 5.

papers.title: Circular Motion: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on circular motion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A body moves in a circle at constant speed. Its acceleration is
questions.explanation:
The changing direction of the velocity gives a centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ towards the centre.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- zero, because its speed is constant: Its direction changes, so its velocity changes and it is accelerating.
- along the tangent in the direction of motion: The velocity is along the tangent; the acceleration points to the centre.
- directed away from the centre: Centripetal means centre-seeking.

options.label: A
options.content: directed towards the centre of the circle

options.label: B
options.content: zero, because its speed is constant

options.label: C
options.content: along the tangent in the direction of motion

questions.stem: A wheel turns at 300 revolutions per minute. What is its angular velocity?
questions.explanation:
$f = 300 \div 60 = 5$ Hz; $\omega = 2\pi f = 10\pi = 31.4\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 rad s⁻¹: That is the frequency in revolutions per second. Multiply by $2\pi$.
- 1885 rad s⁻¹: You forgot to change minutes to seconds.
- 15.7 rad s⁻¹: One revolution is $2\pi$ radians, not $\pi$.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg stone on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at 6 m s⁻¹. What is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation:
$T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{0.5 \times 36}{2} = 9\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.5 N: You used $mv/r$; centripetal force is $mv^2/r$.
- 36 N: You multiplied by the radius instead of dividing.
- 18 N: You forgot the mass of 0.5 kg.

questions.stem: A stone whirled in a horizontal circle on a string is released when the string breaks. It moves off
questions.explanation:
With the centripetal force gone, the stone continues in a straight line in the direction it was moving: along the tangent.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- along the radius, away from the centre: No outward force acts; with no force, it moves straight on along its velocity, which is tangential.
- towards the centre of the circle: With no string, nothing pulls it towards the centre.
- in a smaller circle: Without a centripetal force it cannot keep circling.

options.label: A
options.content: along the radius, away from the centre

options.label: B
options.content: towards the centre of the circle

options.label: D
options.content: along the tangent to the circle at that point

questions.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg rounds a level bend of radius 40 m at 10 m s⁻¹. What friction force is needed between the tyres and the road?
questions.explanation:
$F = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{1000 \times 100}{40} = 2500\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 250 N: You used $mv/r$ instead of $mv^2/r$.
- 2.5 N: You forgot the mass: $v^2/r$ is the acceleration, not the force.
- 4000000 N: You multiplied by the radius.

questions.stem: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
questions.explanation:
$F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$: doubling $r$ divides $F$ by $2^2 = 4$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- half as large: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: double the distance, quarter the force.
- twice as large: Increasing the distance weakens the force.
- four times as large: The force decreases, it does not increase.

questions.stem: A geostationary satellite has a period of
questions.explanation:
It orbits at the same rate as the Earth spins, so it stays above one point on the equator: a period of 24 hours.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1 hour: A satellite close to the Earth takes about 1.5 hours; a geostationary one is much higher.
- 12 hours: To stay above the same point, it must turn with the Earth: once every 24 hours.
- 365 days: That is the Earth's orbit around the Sun.

questions.stem: A body moves in a circle of radius 5 m with angular velocity 4 rad s⁻¹. What is its linear speed?
questions.explanation:
$v = \omega r = 4 \times 5 = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.25 m s⁻¹: You divided the radius by ω; $v = \omega r$.
- 0.8 m s⁻¹: You divided ω by the radius.
- 80 m s⁻¹: That is the centripetal acceleration, $\omega^2 r$.

papers.title: Simple Harmonic Motion: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on simple harmonic motion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A body moves with simple harmonic motion if its acceleration is
questions.explanation:
SHM: $a = -\omega^2 x$, proportional to displacement and always towards the equilibrium position.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- constant and directed towards a fixed point: In SHM the acceleration changes with displacement.
- proportional to its velocity: SHM links acceleration to displacement, not velocity.
- proportional to its displacement and directed away from the fixed point: The restoring acceleration points back towards the fixed point.

options.label: A
options.content: proportional to its displacement from a fixed point and directed towards that point

options.label: B
options.content: constant and directed towards a fixed point

options.label: D
options.content: proportional to its displacement and directed away from the fixed point

questions.stem: A pendulum makes 40 complete oscillations in 60 s. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation:
$f = \dfrac{40}{60} = 0.67\ \text{Hz}$ (period 1.5 s).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.5 Hz: That is the period (60 ÷ 40), not the frequency.
- 2400 Hz: You multiplied the oscillations by the time.
- 40 Hz: That is the number of oscillations, not oscillations per second.

questions.stem: What is the period of a simple pendulum 2.5 m long? (g = 10 m s⁻², take π = 3.14)
questions.explanation:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}} = 2(3.14)\sqrt{0.25} = 3.14\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.57 s: You left out the 2 in $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$.
- 9.93 s: You left out g: the formula is $2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, not $2\pi\sqrt{l}$.
- 12.56 s: You used $\sqrt{g/l}$ instead of $\sqrt{l/g}$.

questions.stem: The period of a simple pendulum does NOT depend on
questions.explanation:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ contains no mass term.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the length of the string: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$: a longer string gives a longer period.
- the acceleration due to gravity: $g$ appears in the formula; a pendulum swings more slowly on the Moon.
- the place where it swings, if g differs there: Different places can have slightly different $g$.

options.label: C
options.content: the place where it swings, if g differs there

questions.stem: For a body moving with SHM, the speed is greatest
questions.explanation:
At the centre the potential energy is least and the kinetic energy greatest.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- at the extreme positions: At the extremes the body stops momentarily.
- halfway between the centre and an extreme: Speed keeps increasing all the way to the centre.
- at the same value everywhere: In SHM the speed changes continuously.

options.label: C
options.content: halfway between the centre and an extreme

questions.stem: A 0.2 kg mass oscillates on a spring of spring constant 20 N m⁻¹. What is the period? (take π = 3.14)
questions.explanation:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2(3.14)\sqrt{\dfrac{0.2}{20}} = 6.28 \times 0.1 = 0.628\ \text{s}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 62.8 s: You used $\sqrt{k/m}$ instead of $\sqrt{m/k}$.
- 0.0628 s: You forgot the square root.
- 0.314 s: You left out the 2.

questions.stem: Resonance occurs when
questions.explanation:
When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, energy is fed in at just the right moments and the amplitude becomes very large.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a body vibrates with decreasing amplitude: That is damping.
- the driving frequency is far from the natural frequency: Then the amplitude stays small.
- a body stops vibrating: Resonance makes the amplitude large, not zero.

options.label: A
options.content: a body vibrates with decreasing amplitude

options.label: B
options.content: the driving frequency is far from the natural frequency

options.label: D
options.content: a body is forced to vibrate at its natural frequency

questions.stem: A body performs SHM with amplitude 0.2 m and angular frequency 5 rad s⁻¹. What is its maximum speed?
questions.explanation:
$v_{max} = A\omega = 0.2 \times 5 = 1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5 m s⁻¹: That is the maximum acceleration, $A\omega^2$.
- 0.04 m s⁻¹: You divided the amplitude by ω.
- 25 m s⁻¹: You squared ω without the amplitude.

papers.title: Work, Energy, and Power: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on work, energy, and power, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A force of 50 N pulls a box 8 m along the floor in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
questions.explanation:
$W = Fs = 50 \times 8 = 400\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 6.25 J: You divided force by distance.
- 58 J: You added force and distance.
- 200 J: You halved the work; $W = Fs$ with no ½.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball moves at 6 m s⁻¹. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation:
$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(2)(36) = 36\ \text{J}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 72 J: You forgot the ½.
- 12 J: You used $mv$ (momentum), not $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.
- 6 J: You forgot to square the speed.

questions.stem: A 60 kg student climbs stairs 5 m high in 10 s. What is her power? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$P = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \dfrac{60 \times 10 \times 5}{10} = 300\ \text{W}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3000 W: That is the work done (energy), not the power.
- 30 W: You left out g: weight = 600 N.
- 120 W: You divided by 25 instead of 10.

questions.stem: A stone falls freely from rest from a height of 45 m. With what speed does it hit the ground? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{900} = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 900 m s⁻¹: That is $v^2$.
- 21.2 m s⁻¹: You forgot the 2: $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ gives $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
- 450 m s⁻¹: You found $gh$ without the 2 or the square root.

questions.stem: In which of these cases is NO work done on the object?
questions.explanation:
Work needs movement in the direction of the force. A load held still does not move.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A woman lifts a bucket of water from the floor to a table.  
  The bucket moves upwards in the direction of the lifting force: work is done.
- A boy pushes a cart along a road.  
  The cart moves in the direction of the push: work is done.
- A crane raises a steel beam.  
  The beam moves upwards: work is done.

options.label: A
options.content: A man holds a heavy load still above his head.

options.label: B
options.content: A woman lifts a bucket of water from the floor to a table.

options.label: C
options.content: A boy pushes a cart along a road.

options.label: D
options.content: A crane raises a steel beam.

questions.stem: In a hydroelectric power station, the main energy change is
questions.explanation:
Water stored high behind a dam has potential energy; it falls and gains kinetic energy, turning turbines that drive generators.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- chemical energy → heat energy → electrical energy: That describes a diesel or coal power station.
- light energy → electrical energy: That describes a solar panel.
- electrical energy → kinetic energy: That describes an electric motor.

options.label: A
options.content: chemical energy → heat energy → electrical energy

options.label: D
options.content: potential energy → kinetic energy → electrical energy

questions.stem: A pump with an input power of 2 kW raises 900 kg of water through 12 m in 60 s. What is its efficiency? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Useful work $= mgh = 900 \times 10 \times 12 = 108\,000$ J. Input $= 2000 \times 60 = 120\,000$ J. Efficiency $= 90\%$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 5400 %: You compared the useful work with the input power, not with the energy input (power × time).
- 0.9 %: You found the fraction but did not multiply by 100.
- 111.1 %: You divided input by output.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation:
Crude oil formed over millions of years and is being used up far faster than it forms.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- solar energy: Sunlight is replaced continuously: renewable.
- hydroelectric energy: Rain refills rivers and dams: renewable.
- wind energy: Wind is renewed by the Sun's heating of the air: renewable.

papers.title: Simple Machines: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on simple machines, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A machine lifts a load of 500 N with an effort of 125 N. What is its mechanical advantage?
questions.explanation:
$\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \dfrac{500}{125} = 4$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.25: You divided the effort by the load.
- 375: You subtracted the effort from the load.
- 625: You added them.

questions.stem: A machine has a velocity ratio of 6 and a mechanical advantage of 4.5. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation:
Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{4.5}{6} \times 100\% = 75\%$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 133.3 %: You divided VR by MA.
- 27 %: You multiplied MA by VR.
- 0.75 %: You found the ratio but did not multiply by 100.

questions.stem: The efficiency of a real machine is always less than 100% because
questions.explanation:
Part of the input work goes into friction (heat) and lifting parts of the machine, so useful output is less than input.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the effort is always smaller than the load: Many machines have effort smaller than load, yet that is not why efficiency is below 100%.
- the velocity ratio is always less than 1: Most machines have a VR greater than 1.
- machines create extra energy: Machines cannot create energy.

options.label: A
options.content: the effort is always smaller than the load

options.label: B
options.content: some work is wasted overcoming friction and lifting moving parts

options.label: C
options.content: the velocity ratio is always less than 1

questions.stem: A wheelbarrow is an example of a
questions.explanation:
The wheel is the fulcrum, the load is in the middle and the effort is at the handles: a second-class lever.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- first-class lever: In a first-class lever the fulcrum is between effort and load; in a wheelbarrow the load is in the middle.
- third-class lever: In a third-class lever the effort is in the middle.
- pulley system: A wheelbarrow has no ropes or pulleys.

questions.stem: A block and tackle has three pulleys in the upper block and two in the lower block. What is its velocity ratio?
questions.explanation:
For a block and tackle, VR = total number of pulleys = 3 + 2 = 5.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3: Count the pulleys in both blocks (or the strands supporting the lower block).
- 2: Count the pulleys in both blocks, not just the lower one.
- 6: You multiplied the numbers of pulleys.

questions.stem: A plank 5 m long is used to roll a drum onto a platform 1.25 m high. What is the velocity ratio of this inclined plane?
questions.explanation:
$\text{VR} = \dfrac{l}{h} = \dfrac{5}{1.25} = 4$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.25: You divided the height by the length.
- 6.25: You multiplied length by height.
- 3.75: You subtracted the height from the length.

questions.stem: A screw jack has a pitch of 0.5 cm and a handle 35 cm long. What is its velocity ratio? (take π = 22/7)
questions.explanation:
$\text{VR} = \dfrac{2\pi a}{p} = \dfrac{2 \times \tfrac{22}{7} \times 35}{0.5} = \dfrac{220}{0.5} = 440$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 70: You used the handle length directly. The effort moves round a circle of circumference $2\pi a$.
- 220: You used $\pi a$ instead of $2\pi a$.
- 110: You used $2\pi a$ but divided by 2 cm instead of 0.5 cm.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic press, the small piston has an area of 4 cm² and the large piston 200 cm². What load can an effort of 60 N support on the large piston?
questions.explanation:
$F_2 = F_1 \times \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = 60 \times \dfrac{200}{4} = 3000\ \text{N}$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1.2 N: You divided instead of multiplying by the area ratio.
- 264 N: You added the areas to the effort.
- 12000 N: You multiplied by the larger area alone.
